title: East Meon Church of England Controlled Primary School: 14 July 2026
text:
Determination
Case reference: VAR2766
Admission Authority: Hampshire County Council for East Meon Church
of England Controlled Primary School
Date of decision: 14 July 2026
Determination
In accordance with section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998, I
approve the proposed variation to the admission arrangements determined by
Hampshire County Council for East Meon Church of England Controlled Primary
School, for 2026.
I determine that for admission in 2026 the published admission number will be five.
The referral
1. Hampshire County Council (the Local Authority or LA) has referred to the adjudicator
a proposal for a variation to the admission arrangements for East Meon Church of England
Controlled Primary School (the School or EMPS) for 2026 (the Arrangements).
2. EMPS is a voluntary controlled primary school for children aged four to eleven years.
It sits within the village of East Meon, west of Petersfield in Hampshire, and is a co-
educational, non-selective school. EMPS has a Church of England religious character, and
the faith body for the School is the Diocese of Portsmouth (the Diocese).
3. The Admission Authority for the School is the Local Authority. As the LA is the
Admission Authority, both terms are used throughout this determination.
4. Parties to the request are the LA, the School and the Diocese.
5. The proposed variation is that the published admission number (PAN), which applies
to the Reception Year (Year R), be reduced from 13 to five. I say more about the current
PAN below.

Jurisdiction and procedure
6. Section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998 (the Act) makes
provision for variations to determined arrangements. Paragraphs 3.6 and 3.7 of the School
Admissions Code (the Code) say (insofar as is relevant here):
“3.6 Once admission arrangements have been determined for a particular school year,
they cannot be revised by the admission authority unless such revision is necessary to
give effect to a mandatory requirement of this Code, admissions law, a determination
of the Adjudicator or any misprint in the admission arrangements. Admission
authorities may propose other variations where they consider such changes to be
necessary in view of a major change in circumstances. Such proposals must be
referred to the Schools Adjudicator for approval, and the appropriate bodies notified.
Where the local authority is the admission authority for a community or voluntary
controlled school, it must consult the governing body of the school before making any
reference.
3.7 Admission authorities must notify the appropriate bodies of all variations”.
7. The Arrangements were determined by the Admission Authority on 12 February
2025. The Admission Authority has provided me with confirmation that the appropriate
bodies have been notified of the proposed variation in line with the Code. I find that the
appropriate procedures were followed, and I am satisfied that the proposed variation is
within my jurisdiction.
8. In the interests of dealing speedily with this request for a variation, I have not
considered other aspects of the Arrangements. Therefore, nothing in this determination
should be taken as indicating that other aspects of the Arrangements do or do not conform
with the requirements relating to admissions.
9. In considering the variation request I have had regard to all relevant legislation and
the Code.
10. The information I have considered in reaching my decision includes:
• the referral from the Admission Authority dated 18 June 2026 and supporting
documents;
• the determined Arrangements for 2026 and the proposed variation to those
Arrangements;
• responses from the LA, the School and the Diocese to my requests for further
information;
• maps, including Google Maps and those showing the location of the School;
• information available on the government website ‘Get Information About Schools’
(GIAS); and
2

• information available on the website of the LA, including the admission
arrangements for EMPS for 2027.
11. There is no formal consultation required for a variation and so parents and others do
not have the opportunity to express their views. Clearly it is desirable that changes to
arrangements are made via the process of determination following consultation as the
consultation process allows those with an interest to express their views. It also allows for
objections to the adjudicator. None of this is afforded by the variation process.
12. I note here that the Arrangements for 2027 have been determined, and a PAN of 15
has been set. Consequently, if I agree to the Admission Authority’s request to vary the
Arrangements for 2026 by reducing the PAN as proposed, it will be for that year only and
will not have a bearing on subsequent years.
Consideration of proposed variation
13. Paragraph 3.6 of the Code (as above) requires that admission arrangements, once
determined, may only be revised, that is changed or varied, if there is a major change of
circumstance or certain other limited and specified circumstances. I will consider below
whether the proposed variation is justified by the change in circumstances.
14. The Admission Authority has proposed that the PAN of the School is reduced from 13
to five for entry to Year R in September 2026. The proposal has the support of the School
and of the Diocese. The referral gave the reason for seeking a variation as follows:
“This application to the Office of the Schools Adjudicator (OSA) seeks approval to
reduce the Published Admission Number (PAN) for East Meon CE Primary from 13
to 5 for September 2026. This reduction is necessary to align the PAN with actual
and projected pupil numbers and to secure the school’s ongoing financial and
organisational viability.
For September 2026, East Meon CE Primary received just 5 offers against a PAN of
13. . . Due to offers being below the PAN, the school is no longer able to
viably operate four classes, and maintaining the current PAN would place significant
and ongoing financial pressure on the school. Implementing the proposed PAN
reduction would enable the school to move to three classes, creating a financially
sustainable structure that more accurately reflects the demand for places.”
15. I pause to consider the current PAN of the School. The referral states, as above, that
the PAN is 13; that is also the figure published in the Arrangements. However, data
accompanying the referral uses a PAN of 15. Assuming there was a typographical error in
the data, I sought clarification from the LA, which stated:
“The PAN of 15 for 2026 is not a typographical error. While increases in PAN are
typically referenced within the annual admissions consultation, the School
Admissions Code does not require such increases to be formally consulted upon. In
this instance, the request to increase the PAN was received after the consultation
3

process had already commenced. Therefore, revised PAN of 15 for 2026 onwards
was agreed.”
16. The LA is correct that increases to PAN may be made without consultation. However,
it is not clear to me whether a PAN of 15 was “agreed”, as the LA has stated, as part of
determining the Arrangements or following their determination.
17. If a PAN of 15 was determined, then the Arrangements should show that figure; they
do not do so. If the LA determined a PAN of 13 and subsequently varied it to 15, as
provided for by Paragraph 3.6 of the Code which allows increases to PAN without referral to
the adjudicator, then the Arrangements should have been revised accordingly. The
Arrangements have not been revised, and I have seen no evidence that such a variation
was agreed by the Admission Authority. Consequently, I consider the PAN to be 13. In the
interest of completeness, I note that paragraph 1.4 of the Code allows for admissions above
the level of the PAN; such admissions do not constitute an increase to the PAN, as stated
in paragraph 1.5 of the Code.
18. I have given careful consideration to the latest available data in order to form a view
about the sufficiency of school places in the local area if the PAN of the School is reduced
from 13 to five. I have also considered the demand for places at the School, the potential
effect of the proposed PAN reduction on meeting parental preference, and whether the
proposed reduction is justified taking into account all relevant circumstances.
19. The Local Authority has a duty to make sure that there are sufficient places for the
children in its area. It uses planning areas, which are geographical areas each containing a
number of schools, for this purpose. In the planning area to which the School belongs, there
are eight schools (including the School) which admit pupils to Year R. Table 1, below,
shows: the sum of the PANs at those schools; and the number of children admitted in each
of 2023, 2024 and 2025. Table 1 also shows the number of children offered a place for
2026 (as of 4 June) and demonstrates the effect on surplus places of reducing the PAN of
the School as has been proposed.

20. The Department for Education document, “Basic need allocations 2026-27 and 2027-
28: Explanatory note on methodology”, refers to the need for two per cent surplus capacity
“to provide an operating margin for local authorities. This helps to support parental choice,
pupil population movement, and general manageability of the system”. From the data in
table 1, I am satisfied that if the PAN of the School were to be reduced to five for 2026,
there would be sufficient places available in the planning area for any children who might be
seeking a Year R place.
21. I will now consider the demand for places at the School. Table 2 shows the number of
first preference applications received, and the number of children admitted in each of 2024
and 2025. It also shows the number of offers made for 2026, as of 4 June.
Table 2: The number of first preference applications for the School for each of 2024,
2025 and 2026; and the number of children admitted or offered a place.

22. The data in table 2 show a fall in the number of first preference applications for 2026.
The data also show that all the children whose parents wanted their child to be admitted to
EMPS in September have been offered a place; the number of offers is significantly below
the PAN. The LA has told me that the five offers made for 2026 comprise four made on
National Offer Day and one made subsequently, I assume to a late applicant.
5

23. The proposed variation would have no effect on parental preference in respect of
applications received as part of the normal admissions process for September 2026.
However, if the proposed variation is approved, then no vacant places will remain at the
School. I cannot, therefore, rule out the possibility that some parents may be disappointed:
namely, any more who may apply late, and parents who seek a place during the course of
the 2026/27 school year.
24. As set out earlier, there are Year R places available within the planning area for 2026.
As of 4 June, three of the other seven schools in that area had vacant spaces. However,
the location of EMPS is, as recorded on GIAS, “smaller rural”. GIAS shows that there are
only two other schools which admit pupils to Year R within three miles of the School, and
that the closest of these is approximately 2.7 miles distant, measured as a straight line. If,
say, a family with a child of Year R age moves into East Meon village during the 2026 / 27
school year they will, if no places remain at EMPS, be obliged to travel some distance to the
next nearest school at which a place is available.
25. The School is affected by the provisions of the School Admissions (Infant Class Size)
(England) Regulations 2012 which require that infant classes (those where the majority of
children will reach the age of five, six or seven during the school year) must not contain
more than 30 pupils with a single qualified schoolteacher except in specific exceptional
circumstances. The infant class size regulations apply to Year R, Year 1 and Year 2.
Children at the School are currently organised into one, single age class for Year R. The
other year groups are organised into mixed-age classes, giving a total of four classes in the
School. If the variation was agreed then all the children could be taught in mixed age
groups, with children in Year R, Year 1 and Year 2 in one class of 30 pupils. This would
result in three total classes with associated financial savings.
26. If the PAN remained at 13 and, say, one further late applicant was admitted to the
School, there would be 31 total children in Year R, Year 1 and Year 2. Those children could
not be taught by a single teacher without breaching the Infant Class Size Regulations and
would need to be taught in two small classes, which is unlikely to be financially viable. As
the PAN would apply to Year R for the entirety of the 2026/27 academic year, the School
would also be required to admit any child whose parents requested a Year R place, until 13
children had been admitted. Even if the number of children admitted on the first day of term
in September 2026 was 5 or fewer and the School was able to operate its planned
organisation of three total classes, any in-year admissions would be likely to necessitate a
reorganisation midway through the year. If, however, the proposed variation was agreed,
the School would be able to plan with certainty.
27. This situation is recognised by the School, which told me:
“As a result of a low existing intake for the 2026 Year R class of only 5 pupils, to
remain financially viable the School will have to reduce the number of its classes
from 4 to 3, resulting in a new combined Years R, 1 and 2 class from September
2026. . .
6

As a result, if the application to vary the 2026 Year R PAN to 5 is not agreed then if
the School were to receive any further pupil intake for the 2026 Year R, the result
could be the School having to open a new class and employ another teacher for a
potentially low level of additional Year R intake. This would place a financial burden
on the School which it cannot afford based on its current pupil numbers; leading to a
fiscal deficit for the School.”
28. The LA provided helpful financial information which it summarised as follows:
“A financial analysis of the school shows that under the original forecast based on a
PAN of 13 the school’s position deteriorates rapidly moving from a surplus of
£45,730 in 2025/26 to a substantial deficit on -£152,416 by 2027/28, reflecting the
cost of running four classes driving increasingly large in-year deficits each year. In
contrast, the revised forecast based on a PAN of 5 significantly slows this decline.
Although still moving into deficit by 2027/28, the cumulative shortfall is much smaller
at -£42,003. The reduction in PAN therefore improves the overall financial position by
approximately £110,000 over the three-year period and delays the onset of a
negative financial position, maintaining a surplus into 2026/27 rather than falling into
deficit earlier. Therefore, the lower PAN and reduction in classes reduces financial
pressure and improves the school’s sustainability.”
29. I have weighed this case carefully. The proposed variation would result in there
being no vacant Year R places at the School. It is possible that families may consequently
be refused admission during the 2026 / 27 school year, and experience difficulties with
travel to alternative schools due to the rurality of the area as I have described above.
However, the size of the School, and the position of its finances, are such that if the PAN is
not reduced then its sustainability may be affected. On balance, I consider that it is
reasonable to conclude that the proposed variation is justified by the circumstances. I
approve the proposed variation to reduce the PAN for 2026 from 13 to five.
30. I note here that reducing the PAN does not reduce the overall capacity of the School
unless accommodation is being removed from the premises. It is not being suggested that
accommodation is being removed and so the physical capacity of the School remains the
same. Reducing the PAN will not change that. What this means is that should there be a
need for the School to admit more children than it currently expects to, there remains the
capacity in the building for it to do so.
31. For the avoidance of doubt, I note the following which was included in a letter sent to
me by the School:
“Please do however note that we are only seeking to reduce the PAN for the 2026
Year R intake (and would like to retain a PAN of 13 for the 2027 Year R intake and
thereafter).”
32. The published, determined arrangements for 2027 state a PAN of 15. As I have said,
my determination has no bearing on that year. Consequently, the PAN of the School for
7

2027 is 15, and may not be reduced unless a proposal for a variation is agreed by the
adjudicator.
Determination
33. In accordance with section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998, I
approve the proposed variation to the admission arrangements determined by Hampshire
County Council for East Meon Church of England Controlled Primary School, for 2026.
34. I determine that for admission in 2026 the published admission number will be five.
Dated: 14 July 2026
Signed:
Schools Adjudicator: Jennifer Gamble
